title: Sudden breathlessness in a 70-year-old man with previous bypass surgery
desc: This station involves a focused history and examination of a 70-year-old retired nurse brought to the ED by ambulance with sudden severe breathlessness after a month of worsening fatigue, orthopnoea and leg swelling. The candidate then interprets his observations, ECG, bloods with a venous gas and a chest X-ray, diagnoses acute cardiogenic pulmonary oedema on a background of heart failure, weighs the differentials (ACS, malignant effusion, infection, PE) and outlines ED management and safety netting.
focus: Acute breathlessness: eliciting heart failure symptoms, excluding the dangerous differentials, reading a chest X-ray of pulmonary oedema with effusions, and managing acute pulmonary oedema in the ED
stem: You are the intern in the Emergency Department of a metropolitan hospital. Mr Josip, a 70-year-old retired nurse, has been brought in by ambulance with shortness of breath that started this morning. He is in an acute bay on a cardiac monitor with an IV cannula in place. A nurse is with you and can carry out your instructions. The nurse has recorded an ECG and sent bloods with a venous blood gas, and a portable chest X-ray has been requested.
tasks: Take a focused history from Mr Josip and perform a focused examination, telling the examiner what you are examining. He is very breathless, so keep your questions targeted (10 minutes).
The examiner will give you his observations, ECG, blood results with a venous gas, and chest X-ray report. Interpret them, then outline your management approach and safety netting (5 minutes).
patient:
Role: You are Mr Josip, a 70-year-old retired nurse. You are not of Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander origin. You are sitting bolt upright on the trolley, leaning forward with your hands on your knees, breathing fast. You can only speak a few words at a time and stop to gasp. You are frightened but you know hospitals well, and you want to cooperate. The examiner gives examination findings from the Exam findings below when the candidate says what they examine.

What the nurse reports at the start (when the candidate asks, or straight away if they do not): "Mr Josip came in by ambulance about 10 minutes ago. The paramedics gave him one GTN tablet under the tongue at about half past nine. The ambulance oxygen was taken off at handover for a room-air set as he was being moved across; I'm about to put him back on. The triage set on room air: resp rate 32, sats 88%, heart rate 108 and regular, BP 186 over 98, temperature 36.9, BGL 11.4, and a repeat at 10:08 was resp rate 34, sats 87%, heart rate 114, BP 184/100. He's on the monitor, the cannula is in, bloods and a venous gas have gone, the ECG is done and the portable X-ray is on its way. What would you like?"

How you change with what the candidate does:

  • If they ask for oxygen, the nurse asks, "What saturation are you aiming for?" With oxygen your sats rise to about 91% and you look a little less blue, but you are still very breathless.
  • If they keep you sitting upright, you say, "Don't lie me down, I can't breathe flat."
  • If they ask for more GTN or a GTN infusion, after a few minutes you breathe slightly more easily, your BP comes down to about 170/92 and your heart rate to about 104.
  • If they ask for CPAP or non-invasive ventilation, the nurse says the CPAP machine is being set up and the senior ED doctor is on the way.
  • If they call the senior ED doctor, the nurse says: "I've called them; they're coming from resus in a few minutes, keep going."
  • If they ask for IV furosemide, the nurse gives it; nothing changes within the station time.
  • If they do nothing for your breathing in the first few minutes, the nurse says, "His sats are down to 85% and his resp rate is 36," and you become harder to understand.
  • If they ask for results now, the examiner says these will be given in Part 2.

Opening line: "I just... can't... get my breath."

History (give only when asked; short phrases):

The breathlessness

  • Onset: it came on suddenly this morning at about 9 am.
  • Character: "Feels like there's a tight band around my chest. I just couldn't breathe."
  • Severity: "I couldn't even walk to the toilet. I had to lean on the wall and gasp for breath."
  • What makes it worse or better: "It was so bad nothing can make it worse." The GTN tablet the ambulance gave you helped a little.
  • Before today: over the past month you have been more tired and more breathless than before.
  • Exercise tolerance: over the last few months you can walk about 200 m before you have to stop. Two years ago you could walk around the block easily.
  • Compared with your heart attack (if asked whether this is like before): "It feels different to my previous heart attack. That was the worst feeling ever."

Other symptoms (only if asked)

  • Lying flat: you usually sleep on 2 pillows. Lying flat makes you more breathless.
  • At night: you wake up at night gasping and have to sit on the edge of the bed.
  • Cough: you have had a smoker's cough for years. For the past week it has been worse, with frothy, white sputum. No yellow or green sputum and no blood.
  • Ankles: both ankles have been swollen, right up to the knees, for the past few weeks. Your shoes feel tight. You do not weigh yourself.
  • Energy: lethargic for about a month.
  • Heart attack symptoms: the tightness is not a pain like your heart attack and does not spread anywhere. "A bit clammy from the effort of breathing, but not the drenching sweat I had with the heart attack." No nausea, no light-headedness, no palpitations.
  • Clot and collapsed lung: no sharp pain when breathing in, no injury or fall, no coughing up blood. You have not been immobile, had no recent operation or long trip, and neither calf is painful. Both legs are swollen the same.
  • Infection: no wheeze, no fever or shivers, no sick contacts.
  • General: no weight loss, no night sweats, appetite is fine.

Past medical history

  • Heart attack 12 years ago.
  • Triple bypass operation 10 years ago.
  • High blood pressure.
  • High cholesterol.
  • Type 2 diabetes.
  • Thyroid removed (thyroidectomy) 30 years ago.

Medications (you take them every day and have not missed any)

  • Metformin.
  • Sitagliptin.
  • Perindopril.
  • Atorvastatin.
  • Tiotropium inhaler, which your GP gave you for your smoker's chest.
  • Thyroxine.
  • No fluid tablets, no aspirin or blood thinners, nothing over the counter (only if asked).
  • No erection tablets such as Viagra (only if asked).

Allergies: none.

Family history: your father died with Alzheimer's disease. Your mother had end-stage kidney disease. You have one sister, who is well.

Social history

  • Smoking: you started at 30 and smoked about 20 a day. After your heart attack you cut down to 4 or 5 a day, which you still smoke.
  • You do not drink alcohol and have never used recreational drugs.
  • You are a retired nurse. You live with your wife. You have 2 sons and 5 grandchildren.
  • You are independent, but for months you have been lacking the energy to do the housework.

Ideas, concerns, expectations: as a retired nurse you wonder whether it is your heart again, but it does not feel like last time. You are worried about your smoking and your lungs. You are frightened of dying and of leaving your wife on her own. You want to be able to breathe, and you want your wife told where you are.

If the candidate asks whether anything else is worrying you, say: "Is it my heart giving out?"

Exam findings (give only when the candidate says what they examine)

  • General: sitting upright, leaning forward, using his neck and shoulder muscles to breathe. Speaking 2 or 3 words at a time. Dusky lips. Slightly sweaty. Nicotine staining on the right fingers. Weight 84 kg.
  • Scars: healed midline sternotomy scar; healed transverse scar low on the front of the neck (thyroidectomy); healed scar along the inside of the left leg (vein harvest).
  • Vital signs: as the nurse reported.
  • Hands: peripheries cool and slightly clammy (vasoconstricted), capillary refill 2 seconds. No clubbing. No asterixis.
  • Pulse: regular, normal volume; rate as the latest set: 114/min before treatment (108/min at triage), or about 104/min if GTN has been given.
  • Blood pressure: as the latest set: 184/100 before treatment (186/98 at triage), or about 170/92 if GTN has been given.
  • JVP: raised, 6 cm above the sternal angle with him sitting at 90°. Hepatojugular reflux positive.
  • Praecordium: apex beat displaced to the 6th intercostal space, anterior axillary line. No heaves or thrills.
  • Heart sounds: first and second heart sounds present with an added third heart sound (gallop rhythm). No murmurs. No pericardial rub.
  • Respiratory: trachea central. Expansion reduced at both bases. Dull to percussion at both bases, up to about the lower third on each side, resonant above. Breath sounds and vocal resonance reduced at both bases. Fine inspiratory crackles above the dullness up to both mid zones. No wheeze, no bronchial breathing.
  • Abdomen: soft. Smooth, mildly tender liver edge 2 cm below the right costal margin. No ascites.
  • Legs: pitting oedema on both legs up to the knees, symmetrical. Mild sacral oedema. Calves soft and non-tender. Foot pulses present but hard to feel through the oedema.

check.x: Professionalism
Performs hand hygiene, introduces self and role, confirms Mr Josip's identity and asks whether he is of Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander origin.

Recognises severe respiratory distress from the nurse's observations and acts before finishing the history: keeps him sitting upright, asks for oxygen with a stated target, and calls the senior ED doctor. Then keeps questions short and closed.
check.d: Credit when oxygen is requested and senior help is called within the first few minutes. Credit 88–92% (smoker on tiotropium) or 92–96% with a plan to reassess; no credit for high-flow oxygen without a target.

check.x: History
Characterises the breathlessness:
check.d: Credit when onset and at least 2 of the other 3 are elicited.

kids.x: Onset: sudden, this morning at about 9 am
Character: a tight band around the chest, unable to breathe
Severity: could not walk to the toilet, leaning on the wall gasping
Background and modifiers: a month of worsening tiredness and breathlessness; nothing makes it worse; the ambulance GTN helped a little

check.x: Establishes the decline in exercise tolerance: about 200 m over the last few months, against walking around the block easily 2 years ago.
Asks about symptoms of heart failure:
check.d: Credit when at least 3 of the 4 are elicited, including orthopnoea or PND and the leg swelling.

kids.x: Orthopnoea (usually sleeps on 2 pillows) and paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea
Smoker's cough, worse for a week, with frothy white sputum
Swelling of both ankles up to the knees for a few weeks

check.x: Asks about features of ACS, including a comparison with his previous heart attack: chest pain or tightness (a tight band that feels different to his MI, which was the worst feeling ever; non-radiating), sweating (clammy from breathing effort only, not like his MI), nausea, light-headedness and palpitations (others absent).
Asks about features of PE and pneumothorax: pleuritic pain, chest injury, haemoptysis, immobility or recent surgery, and unilateral calf pain or swelling (all absent).
Asks about features of an infective exacerbation or pneumonia: yellow or green sputum, wheeze, fever and sick contacts (all absent).
Screens for constitutional symptoms (weight loss, night sweats, appetite) because of his age and smoking (none).
Takes the past medical history: heart attack 12 years ago, triple bypass 10 years ago, hypertension, high cholesterol, type 2 diabetes and thyroidectomy 30 years ago.
check.d: Credit when at least 4 of the 6 are elicited, including the heart attack and the bypass. May ask family history; not required.

check.x: Takes the medication history (metformin, sitagliptin, perindopril, atorvastatin, tiotropium, thyroxine), checks adherence, notes he takes no diuretic, antiplatelet or anticoagulant, and asks about allergies (none).

Takes a social history: quantifies smoking (20 a day from 30 to the heart attack, then 4 to 5 a day; about 30 pack-years), no alcohol or drugs, lives with his wife, independent but without the energy for housework for months.
Explores his ideas, concerns and expectations: wonders if it is his heart, worries about his lungs and smoking, fears dying and leaving his wife, wants to breathe and his wife told.
Examination
General inspection: posture, accessory muscle use, words per breath, cyanosis, sweating, nicotine staining and the surgical scars (sternotomy, thyroidectomy, vein harvest).
Cardiovascular examination for heart failure:
check.d: Credit when the JVP is examined plus at least one of the other two sub-items.

kids.x: Pulse rate and rhythm, BP and peripheral perfusion
Displaced apex beat and auscultation finding a third heart sound, with no murmur or rub

check.x: Respiratory examination finding bibasal dullness with reduced breath sounds (effusions) and fine inspiratory crackles to the mid zones (oedema), with the trachea central and no wheeze.
Examines for fluid overload elsewhere: bilateral pitting oedema to the knees, sacral oedema, tender liver edge, and soft non-tender calves.
Interpretation

Interprets the observations: RR 32 to 34 and SpO2 88 to 87% on room air are in the red zone and worsening, calling for a rapid response (senior ED doctor at the bedside now); systolic BP in the 180s is in the yellow zone (hypertensive); HR is white but tachycardic.
check.d: Credit when RR and SpO2 are identified as red zone and worsening, with immediate escalation; naming the BP and HR zones is not required.

check.x: Interprets the ECG as sinus tachycardia with old anterior Q waves and poor R wave progression, unchanged from the previous ECG, with no ST elevation and no new ischaemic change.

Interprets the NT-proBNP (6200 ng/L) as strongly supporting heart failure, and the single mildly raised troponin (48 ng/L) as myocardial injury that needs a repeat troponin to separate an acute MI from injury due to heart failure.

Interprets the other bloods: impaired renal function (creatinine 124, eGFR 50) to monitor during diuresis; normal WCC with only a small CRP rise (against infection); mild hyponatraemia may also be noted.
check.d: Mild hyponatraemia (133, likely dilutional from congestion) is optional, not required.

check.x: Interprets the venous gas as a mild acidaemia with a raised pCO2 (possible acute hypercapnia) and a mildly raised lactate, so he needs an arterial gas, a lower oxygen target and consideration of NIV.
Reads the chest X-ray: pulmonary oedema, bilateral pleural effusions and cardiomegaly (AP film, sternotomy wires and clips noted for extra credit).
check.d: Credit when the oedema, both effusions and the cardiomegaly are all named.

check.x: Gives the diagnosis as acute pulmonary oedema on a background of heart failure, justified by cardiovascular risk factors and previous MI, orthopnoea, PND, bilateral leg swelling and the X-ray. Names the differentials: ACS (less likely but possible), malignant pleural effusion (age, smoking), infective exacerbation or pneumonia, and PE.
check.d: Credit when the diagnosis is justified with at least 3 supporting features and at least 3 differentials are named, including ACS.

check.x: Management
Escalates now: resus bay or acute bay with continuous cardiac and SpO2 monitoring, senior ED doctor at the bedside, and medical or cardiology registrar involved.
Keeps him sitting upright and titrates oxygen to SpO2 88 to 92% because he is a smoker on tiotropium with a raised venous pCO2, and arranges an arterial gas.
Starts non-invasive ventilation (CPAP, or bilevel NIV given the raised pCO2) for persisting distress and hypoxaemia, and involves ICU if he does not improve or tires.

Gives nitrates for hypertensive pulmonary oedema, after checking for recent PDE5 inhibitor use and no significant aortic stenosis: repeated sublingual GTN, then an IV GTN infusion titrated to symptoms and BP, avoided if systolic BP falls below 90 mmHg.
check.d: Credit for sublingual GTN then IV GTN infusion titrated to BP, held if systolic below 90 mmHg; PDE5 and aortic stenosis check is extra credit, not required.

check.x: Gives an IV loop diuretic (IV furosemide 20 to 40 mg for a diuretic-naive patient (credit up to 80 mg with the renal impairment), repeated or increased by response), with fluid balance charting, urine output monitoring, daily weights and daily UEC and potassium.
check.d: Credit for IV furosemide 20 to 80 mg plus monitoring of renal function/potassium and fluid balance (either).

check.x: Looks for the precipitant and plans for the effusions: serial ECG and troponin, echocardiogram; effusions expected to settle with diuresis, tap or CT if they persist or become one-sided.
Withholds metformin; admits to CCU or HDU under cardiology or general medicine; VTE prophylaxis; nicotine replacement.
check.d: Extra credit, not required: reviews perindopril against BP and renal function; aspirin (300 mg loading if ACS suspected, then 100 mg daily for secondary prevention) unless contraindicated, after discussion with the registrar; states that morphine is not routinely recommended; GP within 1 to 2 weeks and cardiology with the echo.

check.x: Communication and safety netting

Explains in plain words that the heart is not pumping well so fluid has backed up into and around the lungs; answers honestly that the heart tracing shows no new heart attack, but one heart blood test is slightly raised, so a heart attack cannot be ruled out until it is repeated; and that fluid on both sides with fluid in the lungs is most likely from the heart, not cancer, and will be rechecked. Checks understanding.

Tells Mr Josip in plain words to tell the nurse at once, or call 000 after discharge, if he is breathless at rest or lying flat, wakes gasping, has chest pain or tightness, feels faint or has palpitations; and to do daily morning weights, seeing his GP if more than 2 kg over 2 days.

part2.lead: Here are his observations, the ECG the nurse recorded, his blood results with the venous gas, and the portable chest X-ray report.
part2.patient:
Ask these only after the examiner reads question 4, one at a time, short of breath:

  • "Is this another heart attack?"
  • "Is the fluid around my lungs cancer? I've smoked for 40 years."

You are a retired nurse, so you follow most of it, but you want it straight. If the candidate is honest and kind, you settle and agree to the plan. If they brush off the cancer question, ask again.

handover.label: Observations
handover.result: Both sets on room air, before the medical review and before any ED treatment. One GTN tablet was given by the paramedics at about 09:30.
handover.model:
• Read: at triage RR 32 and SpO2 88% on room air are in the red zone; systolic BP 186 is in the yellow zone; HR 108 and temperature 36.9 °C are white. At 10:08 RR 34 and SpO2 87% are still red and worse, HR has risen to 114 (white) and BP stays high at 184/100.
  • Meaning: severe respiratory failure, worsening between triage and review, with hypertension and tachycardia, afebrile: this fits hypertensive acute pulmonary oedema, not shock. A white zone heart rate does not make him safe.
  • Changes: the red zone calls for a rapid response; in the ED that means the senior ED doctor at the bedside now, resus-level monitoring, controlled oxygen, early NIV and nitrates while the BP is high.

rows.note: Triage ATS 2: to acute bay, monitor on, ECG done; pain 2 = chest tightness, non-radiating
Repeat set on RA before medical review (pre-treatment)

handover.label: 12-lead ECG
handover.result:
12-lead ECG of Mr Josip, age 70, recorded at 10:04 today (25 mm/s, 10 mm/mV).

  • Rate: 108/min.
  • Rhythm: sinus tachycardia. Regular, with a normal P wave before every QRS.
  • Axis: normal, about +10°.
  • PR interval: 180 ms.
  • QRS duration: 104 ms. No bundle branch block.
  • QTc: 430 ms (Bazett).
  • ST segments and T waves: no ST elevation in any lead. No ST depression. Shallow T wave inversion in V1 to V3.
  • Other: pathological Q waves in V1 to V3 with poor R wave progression. No pathological Q waves in the inferior or lateral leads.
  • Comparison: previous ECG on file from his cardiology review 2 years ago shows the same Q waves and T wave inversion in V1 to V3, in sinus rhythm at 72/min. The only change is the heart rate.
  • Conclusion: sinus tachycardia; old anterior infarct pattern, unchanged from the previous ECG apart from the rate; no acute ST change.
handover.model:
• Read: sinus tachycardia at 108/min, normal axis and intervals. Q waves with poor R wave progression and T inversion in V1 to V3, all present on the old ECG. No ST elevation or depression and no new change.
  • Meaning: an old anterior infarct, consistent with his MI 12 years ago and a likely ischaemic cardiomyopathy. No STEMI and no arrhythmia (such as AF) to explain the decompensation. An unchanged ECG does not exclude NSTEMI.
  • Changes: no reperfusion pathway; serial ECGs with the repeat troponin; treat the pulmonary oedema now.

handover.label: Bloods and venous blood gas
handover.result: Venous sample collected 10:05, about 1 hour after the breathlessness began. Repeat troponin due at 3 hours.
handover.model:
• Read: NT-proBNP 6200 ng/L, well above the 900 ng/L rule-in level for his age. hs-troponin I 48 ng/L, above the male 99th percentile of 34, a single value. Creatinine 124 with eGFR 50, urea 10.8, sodium 133. Albumin, liver tests, TSH, Hb and WCC normal; CRP 14. Venous pH 7.31 with pCO2 56, normal bicarbonate, lactate 2.4, glucose 11.6.
  • Meaning: strong support for acute heart failure. Myocardial injury is present, but one value cannot separate an acute MI from strain on a failing heart. Mild hyponatraemia (133), likely dilutional from congestion; monitor sodium with diuresis. The normal albumin and liver tests argue against nephrotic or liver causes of oedema; normal TSH and WCC argue against thyroid disease and infection as precipitants. The gas suggests acute hypercapnia.
  • Changes: repeat troponin; arterial gas; oxygen target 88 to 92% and early NIV; withhold metformin; monitor renal function and potassium during diuresis.

rows.n: acute HF unlikely below 300; age 50-75 rule-in above 900

handover.label: Portable chest X-ray
handover.result:
Examination: chest X-ray, portable AP erect (sitting), 10:20.

Clinical details: 70-year-old man with sudden severe breathlessness, orthopnoea and bilateral leg oedema. Previous MI and CABG. Smoker. SpO2 88% on room air.

Findings:

  • Lines and devices: ECG electrodes. Median sternotomy wires and mediastinal surgical clips from previous coronary artery bypass grafting.
  • Lungs: diffusely increased interstitial markings throughout both lungs, with perihilar haziness, upper lobe venous diversion and septal (Kerley B) lines in both mid and lower zones above the effusions, consistent with pulmonary oedema. No focal consolidation. No discrete mass is seen, although the lower zones are partly obscured.
  • Pleura: bilateral pleural effusions, moderate in size, with loss of both hemidiaphragm silhouettes and both cardiophrenic angles. No pneumothorax.
  • Heart and mediastinum: the heart is enlarged, even allowing for the AP projection. Trachea central.
  • Bones and soft tissues: no acute bony abnormality.

Conclusion: pulmonary oedema with bilateral pleural effusions and cardiomegaly, in keeping with congestive cardiac failure. Post-CABG. Recommend follow-up imaging after treatment.
handover.model:
• Read: an AP portable film. Diffusely increased interstitial markings with upper lobe diversion and Kerley B lines (pulmonary oedema). Bilateral pleural effusions with loss of both hemidiaphragm silhouettes and both cardiophrenic angles. Enlarged heart. Sternotomy wires and clips. No consolidation, no pneumothorax.
  • Meaning: acute pulmonary oedema on a background of heart failure, matching the crackles, bibasal dullness, raised JVP and leg oedema. Oedema in the lung tissue and fluid in the pleural space coexist. Bilateral, symmetrical effusions with oedema are most likely transudates from heart failure rather than malignancy.
  • Changes: treat as APO now. Repeat the film after diuresis; tap or CT chest if an effusion persists or becomes one-sided, given his age and smoking.

ask: You are now calling the medical registrar. Please give an ISBAR handover of Mr Josip, including your interpretation of these results.
What is your most likely diagnosis, and what else would you consider? Justify your answer.
Outline your management of Mr Josip now, here in the emergency department.
Mr Josip asks whether this is another heart attack and whether the fluid is cancer. Answer him in plain words, then tell him the warning signs he must report.
expect:
• Identify: self, ED intern; Mr Josip, 70, retired nurse.
  • Situation: acute pulmonary oedema; red zone RR 34, SpO2 87% on room air before treatment, worsening between triage and review; BP 184/100, HR 114.
  • Background: sudden breathlessness at 9 am after a month of worsening breathlessness, orthopnoea, PND, frothy sputum and leg oedema to the knees; MI 12 years ago, CABG 10 years ago, hypertension, T2DM, about 30 pack-years and on tiotropium; no diuretic or anticoagulant; no allergies.
  • Assessment: ECG sinus tachycardia, old anterior Q waves, no acute change; NT-proBNP 6200 supports HF; troponin 48, single value; creatinine 124, eGFR 50; WCC normal, CRP 14; VBG pH 7.31, pCO2 56 – needs ABG; CXR interstitial oedema, bilateral effusions, cardiomegaly.
  • Recommendation: controlled oxygen, GTN and IV furosemide started; please review now for NIV and admission to CCU or HDU.

Acute cardiogenic pulmonary oedema on a background of heart failure (likely ischaemic): previous MI and CABG, hypertension, diabetes, smoking; a month of reduced exercise tolerance, orthopnoea, PND, frothy sputum, bilateral oedema; raised JVP, S3, crackles; NT-proBNP 6200; CXR oedema, effusions, cardiomegaly.

  • ACS (NSTEMI) as the precipitant: for: previous MI, troponin 48; against: chest tightness unlike his MI and non-radiating, no nausea or drenching sweat like his MI, unchanged ECG. Repeat troponin.
  • Malignant pleural effusion: for: age 70, 40 years of smoking; against: bilateral, with oedema, no weight loss.
  • Infective COPD exacerbation or pneumonia: for: worse cough for a week, on tiotropium; against: white frothy sputum, no fever or wheeze, normal WCC, no consolidation.
  • PE: against: no pleuritic pain, haemoptysis or immobility; symmetrical leg swelling.

1. Escalate and support: senior ED doctor at the bedside, continuous monitoring, medical or cardiology registrar; keep him upright; oxygen titrated to SpO2 88 to 92% (smoker on tiotropium, raised venous pCO2); arterial gas.
  2. NIV: CPAP, or bilevel NIV given the raised pCO2, for ongoing distress and hypoxaemia; ICU if he fails.
  3. Nitrates: sublingual GTN, then IV GTN infusion titrated to symptoms and BP; hold if systolic below 90 (check PDE5 inhibitors and aortic stenosis).
  4. IV furosemide 20 to 40 mg (diuretic-naive; up to 80 mg credited with the renal impairment), repeated by response; fluid balance, UEC and potassium.
  5. Precipitant and effusions: serial ECG and troponin, echocardiogram; effusions should settle with diuresis, tap or CT if they persist or become one-sided.
  6. Withhold metformin; aspirin (300 mg loading if ACS suspected, then 100 mg daily for secondary prevention) unless contraindicated, after discussion with the registrar; admit to CCU or HDU under cardiology or medicine; VTE prophylaxis; nicotine replacement.

• Plain words: the heart is not pumping strongly enough, so fluid has backed up into the lungs and collected around them; that is why he cannot breathe or lie flat. Checks understanding.
  • Heart attack? The heart tracing has not changed; one blood test is slightly up and is being repeated.
  • Cancer? Fluid on both sides with fluid in the lungs is most likely from the heart; it will be re-checked after treatment, with a sample or scan if it does not clear.
  • Red flags (000): breathless at rest or lying flat, waking gasping, chest pain, fainting, palpitations.
  • Self-care: daily morning weights; GP if more than 2 kg over 2 days.

ddx.dx: Acute cardiogenic pulmonary oedema on a background of heart failure (likely ischaemic cardiomyopathy), with bilateral pleural effusions
ddx.for: Previous MI and CABG with hypertension, diabetes and smoking, a month of falling exercise tolerance, orthopnoea, PND, frothy sputum and leg oedema to the knees, a raised JVP with an S3, NT-proBNP 6200 and a chest X-ray showing oedema, bilateral effusions and cardiomegaly.

ddx.dx: Acute coronary syndrome (NSTEMI) precipitating heart failure
ddx.for: He has had an MI, describes a tight band around the chest and has a mildly raised troponin of 48 ng/L.
ddx.against: Chest tightness unlike his MI and non-radiating, no nausea or drenching sweat like his MI, unchanged ECG.

ddx.dx: Malignant pleural effusion from lung cancer
ddx.for: He is 70 and has smoked for 40 years, about 30 pack-years.
ddx.against: The effusions are bilateral with pulmonary oedema and heart failure signs, and he has no weight loss, night sweats or haemoptysis.

ddx.dx: Infective exacerbation of COPD or community-acquired pneumonia
ddx.for: His smoker's cough has been worse for a week and he uses tiotropium.
ddx.against: The sputum is white and frothy, he has no fever or wheeze, the WCC is normal, the CRP only slightly raised and there is no consolidation on X-ray.

ddx.for: Sudden-onset breathlessness with hypoxia and tachycardia.
ddx.against: No pleuritic pain, haemoptysis, immobility or recent surgery, the leg swelling is symmetrical with soft calves, and heart failure explains the whole picture.

ddx.for: Sudden breathlessness in a long-term smoker.
ddx.against: No pleuritic pain or injury, the trachea is central, both bases are dull rather than hyperresonant, and the X-ray shows no pneumothorax.

guide:
In Part 1, the nurse gives the triage observations at the start. Mr Josip is very breathless and answers in short phrases. A good candidate acts on the red zone observations (sits him up, controlled oxygen, senior help) before finishing the history, and that earns item 3. Give examination findings only when the candidate says what they examine. If the candidate asks for the ECG, bloods or X-ray in Part 1, say they will be given in Part 2. In Part 2, hand over all four results, then ask the four questions in order. Mr Josip asks his questions after question 4 is read.

A high-performing candidate characterises the sudden breathlessness against a month of decline, elicits orthopnoea, PND, frothy sputum and bilateral leg swelling, and asks targeted questions to rule out ACS, PE, pneumothorax, infection and malignancy. They take the full medication list and the smoking history, and examine for a raised JVP, S3, bibasal crackles and effusions, and oedema. In Part 2 they read the X-ray systematically, including the effusions and the sternotomy wires. They take a single raised troponin as needing a repeat, and they see the raised venous pCO2 and lower the oxygen target. They start NIV, nitrates and IV furosemide, withhold metformin, and admit him. They answer the cancer question honestly.

A borderline candidate takes a generic breathlessness history, misses the orthopnoea or the leg swelling, and does not examine the JVP or the legs. They may call the X-ray "pneumonia", miss the effusions, give high-flow oxygen without a target, or diagnose MI from the troponin alone. Lying him flat, giving no treatment for the oedema, or failing to escalate red zone observations is a serious safety concern.
explain:
Diagnosis: acute cardiogenic pulmonary oedema on a background of heart failure

Acute pulmonary oedema (APO) is fluid building up quickly in the lung tissue, which impairs gas exchange. It usually comes from acute left heart failure: pressure rises in the pulmonary veins and capillaries and pushes fluid out of them. Non-cardiogenic causes include ARDS (sepsis, pneumonia, aspiration), fluid overload in renal failure, and opioid or neurogenic causes. Mr Josip's sudden breathlessness this morning came after a month of decline. Over that month he had less energy, could walk only 200 m, slept on 2 pillows, woke at night gasping, had frothy sputum and developed leg swelling up to the knees. With his previous MI, CABG, hypertension, diabetes and smoking, the most likely cause is an ischaemic cardiomyopathy that has now decompensated.

The history and examination

  • Heart failure symptoms: exertional dyspnoea and falling exercise tolerance, orthopnoea, PND, frothy (sometimes pink) sputum, ankle swelling, weight gain and fatigue.
  • Dangerous differentials to ask about: ACS (chest pain, sweating, nausea, light-headedness, palpitations), pneumothorax (pleuritic pain, injury), PE (pleuritic pain, haemoptysis, immobility, a swollen calf), an infective exacerbation of COPD (purulent sputum, wheeze, fever, sick contacts) and malignancy (weight loss, night sweats).
  • Precipitants: ischaemia, arrhythmia (especially AF), uncontrolled hypertension, infection, non-adherence, salt or fluid excess, anaemia, thyroid disease and medicines that retain fluid.
  • Signs: tachypnoea, hypoxia, a raised JVP, a displaced apex, an S3 gallop, bibasal crackles and peripheral oedema. Pulmonary oedema (in the lung tissue) and pleural effusion (in the pleural space) often coexist. Oedema gives fine inspiratory crackles; an effusion gives stony dullness with reduced breath sounds and vocal resonance.

Interpreting the results

  • Observations: RR and SpO2 in the red zone and worsening call for a rapid response. Hypertension (yellow zone) points to hypertensive APO, which responds well to nitrates.
  • ECG: sinus tachycardia with old anterior Q waves, unchanged from before. No STEMI and no AF.
  • Natriuretic peptide: NT-proBNP below 300 ng/L makes acute heart failure unlikely. Above the age-adjusted cut-off (900 ng/L at age 50 to 75) supports it.
  • Troponin: it is often raised in acute heart failure. A single raised value is myocardial injury; serial testing shows whether there is a rise and fall typical of an acute MI.
  • Other bloods: creatinine 124 (eGFR 50) with no baseline on file needs monitoring during diuresis. Normal albumin and liver tests argue against hypoalbuminaemic causes of oedema (nephrotic syndrome, liver disease). A normal TSH on thyroxine makes thyroid disease an unlikely precipitant. A normal WCC with only a small CRP rise argues against infection.
  • Venous gas: a raised pCO2 with acidaemia in a smoker on tiotropium suggests acute hypercapnia. Confirm with an arterial gas; it calls for a target SpO2 of 88 to 92% and favours NIV.
  • Chest X-ray: on an AP film, look for interstitial oedema (upper lobe diversion, Kerley B lines, perihilar haziness), effusions (loss of the hemidiaphragm silhouettes), cardiomegaly, and clues to the history (sternotomy wires and clips). Exclude consolidation and pneumothorax.

Management (Heart Foundation and CSANZ heart failure guideline, eTG)

  1. Resuscitate and escalate: sit him upright, give continuous monitoring and get senior help.
  2. Oxygen only for hypoxaemia, titrated (TSANZ): 92 to 96% usually, but 88 to 92% where there is a risk of hypercapnia, as in COPD.
  3. Non-invasive ventilation (CPAP, or bilevel NIV when hypercapnic) for respiratory distress or hypoxaemia despite oxygen. It reduces the work of breathing and the need for intubation. Involve ICU if he fails NIV.
  4. Nitrates reduce preload and afterload and are most useful when BP is high: sublingual GTN, then an IV infusion titrated to symptoms and BP. GTN 300 to 600 microgram sublingually (or 400 microgram spray), repeated every 5 minutes; IV GTN infusion starting at about 5 to 10 microgram/min, titrated up every 3 to 5 minutes to symptoms and BP (per eTG). Check first for recent PDE5 inhibitor use and significant aortic stenosis. Avoid them in hypotension (systolic below 90 mmHg).
  5. IV loop diuretic for fluid overload: furosemide IV, with the dose based on previous diuretic use, then adjusted to the response. Monitor urine output, fluid balance, daily weights, renal function and potassium.
  6. Medicines: withhold metformin during hypoxia, hypoperfusion and impaired renal function. Review the ACE inhibitor against BP and renal function. Routine morphine is not recommended. He takes no antiplatelet despite his MI and bypass: under the Australian ACS guideline, aspirin is expected for suspected ACS (300 mg loading) and for secondary prevention (100 mg daily) unless contraindicated, so discuss starting it with the registrar.
  7. Find the cause: serial ECG and troponin, and an echocardiogram for LV ejection fraction, valves and wall motion. The ejection fraction decides long-term guideline-directed therapy. For reduced ejection fraction this means an ACE inhibitor or ARNI, a beta-blocker, a mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist and an SGLT2 inhibitor, started and up-titrated once he is stable.
  8. The effusions: bilateral effusions with oedema in heart failure are usually transudates and settle with diuresis. A one-sided, persistent or atypical effusion needs a diagnostic tap (Light's criteria, cytology) and CT, especially in an older smoker, where a malignant effusion has to be considered.
  9. Disposition: admit under cardiology or general medicine, to CCU or HDU while he needs NIV, with VTE prophylaxis and nicotine replacement.

Safety netting and follow-up

Before discharge, Mr Josip needs to know to call 000 for breathlessness at rest or lying flat, waking gasping, chest pain, fainting or palpitations. He should weigh himself every morning and see his GP if his weight rises by more than 2 kg over 2 days or the swelling or breathlessness worsens. He needs a GP review within 1 to 2 weeks of discharge, cardiology follow-up with the echo, a heart failure management program and cardiac rehabilitation. Stopping smoking (Quitline) and vaccinations are part of the plan. His secondary prevention needs review too, since he takes no antiplatelet or beta-blocker after his MI and bypass.
points: Ask every breathless patient about orthopnoea, PND, frothy sputum, ankle swelling and falling exercise tolerance, and examine the JVP, heart sounds, lung bases and legs.

Pulmonary oedema and pleural effusions often coexist in heart failure: oedema gives crackles, an effusion gives stony dullness with reduced breath sounds. Bilateral effusions with oedema are usually transudates and settle with diuresis.
Read the chest X-ray systematically: AP or PA, interstitial oedema (upper lobe diversion, Kerley B lines), effusions, heart size, and devices such as sternotomy wires that tell the history.
A raised NT-proBNP supports acute heart failure. A single raised troponin is myocardial injury and needs serial testing before an acute MI is diagnosed.

Manage APO with the patient upright, oxygen titrated to target (88 to 92% if at risk of hypercapnia), early NIV, nitrates while BP allows, and an IV loop diuretic; withhold metformin and do not give morphine routinely.

Safety-net with daily weights (more than 2 kg over 2 days: see the GP), 000 for breathlessness at rest or chest pain, and follow-up with the GP, cardiology, a heart failure program and quit-smoking support.
